Furness
FUR-nus
n. (the Lancashire Cistercian abbey founded in 1127, second only to Fountains in wealth among English Cistercian houses)
From Old Norse Futharnes, the headland by the rump-shaped island, from futh and nes, a headland.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Furness Abbey stands in a sheltered valley on the Lancashire peninsula between Morecambe Bay and the Duddon, founded in 1127 by Stephen, later king, for monks of Savigny who joined the Cistercian order in 1147. It became the second richest Cistercian house in England after Fountains, holding the whole of the Furness peninsula, the iron ore of Low Furness, fisheries, granges, ferry rights over the sands and a share of the Isle of Man's church. Its abbots ran a small state, treated with the Scots who raided them in 1316, and were lords of the manor over tenants who owed them labour. It surrendered in 1537, the first great abbey to go, after its monks were implicated in the Pilgrimage of Grace. The dictionary records Furness for the arc of it. Monks who had come north under a rule of poverty ended as the chief ironmasters and landlords of a county, and the New Testament's warnings about wealth are addressed to exactly that process: they that will be rich fall into a snare, and the love of money is a root from which men have erred from the faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rich as having abundant possessions; a snare as a device for catching; a lust as an eager desire; to drown as to overwhelm in water; and perdition as utter destruction.

expand to see more

RICH, a. Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods or money; abundant in materials.

SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds, by the leg; anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.

LUST, n. Longing desire; eagerness to possess or enjoy; concupiscence; evil propensity.

DROWN, v.t. To overwhelm in water; to overflow; to deluge; to immerse and suffocate in water.

PERDITION, n. Entire loss or ruin; utter destruction; the utter loss of the soul or of final happiness.

Key Scripture

1Ti 6:9 — "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition."

1Ti 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Pro 23:4 — "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom."

Luk 12:15 — "And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."

Modern Corruption

Lancashire Cistercian abbey of 1127, second richest of the order in England, lord of the whole Furness peninsula; surrendered in 1537.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that wealth is a danger described in Scripture as a trap rather than merely as a distraction. Paul uses the imagery of snaring and drowning: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9), and he names the root of the failure without naming money itself as evil, “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10).

The live temptation for an order founded on poverty is to accept endowments faithfully and end up a landlord, which is the history of nearly every Cistercian house in Britain. Solomon gives the plain instruction that a granting charter never contains: “Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom” (Pro 23:4). Christ, asked to settle an inheritance, refused the case and gave the reason: “Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). Furness held a peninsula and surrendered first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ploutos (G4149), riches; Greek pagis (G3803), a snare; Greek bythizo (G1036), to sink or drown; Greek apoleia (G0684), destruction.

expand to see more

Greek pagis (G3803) — a trap, a snare; “fall into temptation and a snare”, 1 Timothy 6:9.

Greek bythizo (G1036) — to sink, to plunge; “which drown men in destruction and perdition”, 1 Timothy 6:9.

Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of silver; “the love of money is the root of all evil”, 1 Timothy 6:10.

Hebrew yaga (H3021) — to toil, to weary oneself; “Labour not to be rich”, Proverbs 23:4.

Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, greed; “beware of covetousness”, Luke 12:15.

Usage

"“they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9) — a monastic trajectory."

"“Labour not to be rich” (Pro 23:4) — absent from every charter."

"“beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15) — Christ declining an inheritance case."
